strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing the limitations of hand-engineered tool APIs in SWE agents with timely focus on computer-use paradigms

Comprehensive and well-designed environment supporting multiple languages (8), modalities (text/image/video/audio), and rich IDE tools with proper infrastructure (Docker, checkpointing, gymnasium API)

Extensive benchmark with 5400 instances across 15 diverse tasks from 13 existing datasets plus 2 novel contributions, with principled curation across task types and a lightweight variant for accessibility

Thorough and honest experimental analysis evaluating multiple VLMs with systematic failure mode analysis, clear documentation of limitations, and valuable insights from 'assisted' experiments showing up to 13.3% improvement with proper tools
Clear identification and documentation of current model limitations including visual grounding failures, file editing difficulties, and insufficient IDE tool usage with concrete examples
Solid technical execution with proper infrastructure design, detailed implementation descriptions, comprehensive appendices, and promised reproducibility resources
weaknesses: Core thesis significantly undermined by results showing computer-use agents achieve only 10.2% vs 46.8% with API tools—a 4.6× gap suggesting the approach fundamentally struggles without structured tool interfaces, which validates rather than challenges the tool-based paradigm
Evaluation limited to 300 of 5400 instances (PwP-Bench-Lite) due to computational constraints, limiting confidence in result generalization and reducing the benchmark's practical impact

Unfair comparisons with prior work using different trajectory lengths (55% on SWE-Bench achieved with longer trajectories vs PwP's 20-step limit), model versions, and computational budgets, though acknowledged, still presented prominently

Limited technical novelty—primarily combines existing components (computer-use agents, unified benchmarks) into an SWE-specific environment without fundamental algorithmic or methodological innovations

Critical unresolved problems: visual grounding issues remain fundamentally unsolved beyond Set-of-Marks (existing technique); no novel solutions proposed despite this being identified as the primary bottleneck

Insufficient root cause analysis of why computer-use dramatically underperforms—unclear whether the limitation is the paradigm itself, implementation details, or model training, making it hard to assess future viability

Design choices lack justification: 20-step trajectory limit appears arbitrary and could disadvantage computer-use approaches; no sensitivity analysis provided; task selection criteria could be more explicit

Evaluation metric concerns: macro-averaging across heterogeneous metrics from different datasets (accuracy, F1, pass@k operating at different scales) may not be meaningful; should report task-specific results more prominently

Missing critical comparisons: no evaluation of how existing tool-based agents perform when adapted to PwP, preventing assessment of whether tool-based paradigm is inherently superior or better suited to training

Incomplete trade-off analysis: paper doesn't thoroughly discuss how tool-based approaches provide structure/interpretability/efficiency while computer-use trades these for generality, or clarify when each paradigm is preferable
Generalization concerns: VSCode-specific design limits transferability to other IDEs; IDE-specific shortcuts may reduce long-term value as tools evolve
Code/data release link missing ('We release code and data at [blank]'), affecting reproducibility claims despite other documentation efforts

strengths: Comprehensive benchmark design covering diverse SWE tasks across multiple languages, modalities, and domains with 5400 instances
Well-engineered environment with good infrastructure (Docker sandboxing, state checkpointing, gymnasium interface)
Honest and thorough analysis of agent limitations with concrete visual examples of failure modes
Timely research direction investigating computer-use agents as alternative to tool-based SWE agents
Multiple evaluation configurations testing different agent types and action spaces
weaknesses: Critical evaluation gap: Only 300/5400 instances (5.6%) actually evaluated due to computational constraints, severely undermining confidence in empirical claims and statistical significance

Main thesis contradicted by empirical results: When agents gain explicit tool access, performance jumps from 10.2% to 46.8%, and hand-engineered APIs improve performance by up to 56% (Table 4), which supports rather than challenges the tool-based paradigm
Weak empirical results on claimed paradigm: 10.2% accuracy for pure computer-use agents makes practical deployment questionable, while 46.8% with tools suggests hybrid approaches are necessary

Severe single-model dependency: Only Claude achieves reasonable performance; GPT-4o and Gemini-Flash show dramatically lower accuracy (5.3-32.3% and 1.2-8.9% respectively), without investigation into why or how to address this

Limited novelty: Primarily an infrastructure/benchmark contribution without novel methods, agent architectures, or training approaches; conceptually similar to existing environments (OSWorld, WindowsAgentArena)

Fundamental visual grounding and file editing problems identified but unaddressed: Paper documents extensive failures (Figures 7-12) but proposes no solutions, only noting these are 'important directions for future work'

Unfair comparisons with prior work: SoTA results used longer trajectories, different model versions, and specialized tools; paper acknowledges but still emphasizes competitive claims without proper caveats

Set-of-Marks dependency: Agents require HTML annotation aids to achieve even 10.2% performance, indicating vision models cannot handle raw screenshots effectively—a fundamental limitation that undermines computer-use claims
Missing critical analysis: No investigation of why Claude outperforms other models by 8-40%, no ablation studies on environment design, no systematic analysis of which task types suit which paradigms

Arbitrary design choices not well-justified: 20-step limit chosen without justification; prior work achieved better SWE-Bench results (55%) with longer trajectories, making direct comparison problematic

strengths: Clear problem motivation: compelling argument for why tool-based paradigm limits generalization and scalability, with well-motivated computer-use alternative
Comprehensive, well-designed benchmark: 5400 instances across 15 diverse tasks, 8 languages, multiple modalities, and both code/non-code SWE activities
Solid environment design: expressive observation/action spaces, native IDE tool support without hand-engineering, strong infrastructure (Docker, checkpointing, gymnasium API)
Comprehensive empirical evaluation: multiple agent types, five VLMs tested, honest reporting including strong baselines

Valuable analysis: well-illustrated visual grounding failures, quantified performance gaps (10.2% → 46.8%), assisted experiments showing 13.3% improvement potential, actionable insights on future directions
Good reproducibility: implementation details documented, code/data release promised, multiple interaction modes supported, PwP-Bench-Lite for rapid experimentation
Effective positioning: clear differentiation via Tables 1-2, comprehensive related work, acknowledges both innovations and limitations compared to existing work
Will be valuable resource for research community enabling standardized SWE agent evaluation across languages, modalities, and task types
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty in environment design: computer-use agents in visual environments well-established (OSWorld, WindowsAgentArena); main contribution is SWE-specific focus and benchmark, not novel mechanisms

Evaluation restricted to PwP-Bench-Lite (300 instances) due to computational constraints; full 5400-instance benchmark unevaluated, limiting benchmark contribution validation and potentially affecting generalization

Highly skewed model performance undermines generalizability: only Claude achieves 46.8%; other models achieve 8.9-32.3%, suggesting findings may be Claude-specific rather than paradigm-level insights; limited open-source model evaluation

Weak empirical support for computer-use paradigm: best results (46.8%) require file/bash API access, not 'pure' computer-use; pure computer-use achieves only 10.2%, with Set-of-Marks partially violating visual-only interaction framing

Limited statistical rigor: only one significance test reported; no confidence intervals or error bars; small sample sizes (20 per task); comparisons with prior work complicated by different experimental settings

Analysis could be deeper: visual grounding failures somewhat expected; insufficient investigation of why Claude outperforms competitors by 14-28%; only 4 datasets in 'assisted' experiment; no systematic error categorization or inter-task generalization analysis

Reproducibility gaps: code/data not released (incomplete URL); VSCode modifications not fully documented; task evaluation protocols from heterogeneous datasets unclear; Docker configuration specifics missing

Screenshot observation space limitations: computationally expensive, poor scaling to high resolutions; Set-of-Marks adds complexity; more efficient representations unexplored; limits applicability to resource-constrained settings

Benchmark composition underspecified: no inter-rater agreement validation; macro-averaging heterogeneous metrics obscures patterns; General-SWE dataset composition/evaluation unclear; no task difficulty analysis

strengths: Well-motivated contribution establishing software engineering as an important domain for evaluating computer-use agents

Comprehensive, well-engineered environment (PwP) with expressive action/observation spaces, full IDE tooling access, multimodal support across 14 languages, and reproducible Docker-based infrastructure
Substantial benchmark (PwP-Bench) unifying 15 diverse SWE tasks from 13 existing datasets plus 2 new ones, spanning multiple task categories and modalities
Thorough empirical evaluation with multiple agent designs, 9 model variants, and detailed failure mode analysis identifying concrete limitations (visual grounding, tool usage)
Clear quantitative findings showing dramatic performance gap (22.9% visual → 50.7% with APIs) and actionable insights for future work
Strong infrastructure design with state checkpointing, gymnasium interface, and commitment to open-source release enabling future research
Detailed qualitative analysis with concrete failure examples, including assisted experiments showing 13.3% potential gains from better tool use
weaknesses: Main evaluation limited to PwP-Bench-Lite (300 instances, 5.5% of 5,400 full benchmark) due to computational constraints, raising generalizability concerns and making claims about the full benchmark speculative

Significant step budget limitations (20 steps for main experiments) with only limited 250-step results for 1 model on 3 datasets; unclear how much performance is artificially suppressed for longer-horizon SWE-Bench tasks

Weak specialized baseline: mini-sweagent (48.8%) used in main paper while SOTA ranges 74-75%, making headline claims that CUAs 'approach specialized agents' misleading; SOTA comparison relegated to appendix
Set-of-Marks (SoM) DOM augmentations presented as standard but represent significant assistance; unclear performance degradation without SoM, and their necessity contradicts 'pure visual' positioning
File/Bash API comparisons claim operations are 'theoretically' performable visually, yet the 2.2x performance gap (22.9% vs 50.7%) suggests fundamental differences that aren't fully analyzed
Minimal statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing on most results except one McNemar's test; visual grounding error analysis based on only 20 manual trajectories
Metric aggregation using 'macro averages' across orthogonal metrics from different datasets obscures patterns; datasets with vastly different difficulties weighted equally
Limited methodological novelty: environment + benchmark + evaluation work without novel agent architectures, training methods, or algorithmic contributions limits impact for methods-focused venues

strengths: Comprehensive benchmark with 5400 diverse instances spanning 15 SWE tasks, 14 languages, and multiple modalities
Well-engineered environment with expressive action/observation spaces, execution-based verification, and solid infrastructure (Docker, checkpointing, gymnasium API)
Extensive model evaluation covering 9+ models including open-weight and closed-weight variants with UI-specific training
Concrete failure mode analysis with specific examples of visual grounding errors, UI element misidentification, and state comprehension issues
Clear commitment to reproducibility through promised open-source release and detailed implementation details in appendices
Good presentation with effective use of visualizations and qualitative examples of agent behavior
weaknesses: Severely underpowered evaluation: only 300 of 5400 instances (5.5%) evaluated due to budget constraints, undermining the value of creating such a large benchmark
Artificial step budget limitation: 20-step maximum appears constraining; appendix results show improvements with 250 steps, suggesting main results are suboptimal
Limited technical novelty: core contribution is essentially 'run VSCode in Docker'—incremental over OSWorld, WindowsAgentArena, and other OS environments

Weak and unfair baseline comparisons: only mini-sweagent directly evaluated; acknowledged comparisons to other agents use different experimental settings; the ~50.7% vs 48.8% near-equivalence undermines the central research question rather than answering it
Only 2 new tasks created (40 total instances); remaining tasks are adaptations of existing benchmarks, limiting novelty in task design

Shallow failure mode analysis: manual inspection of only 20 trajectories lacks statistical rigor; no ablation studies to isolate causes of visual grounding failures; findings (visual grounding is hard, tool usage is hard) are expected and align with prior web/OS agent work

Problematic result aggregation: macro-averaging accuracy across 15 diverse tasks (SQL, chart generation, theorem proving) is methodologically questionable; high variance (0-100%) suggests averaging obscures important patterns
Limited actionable insights: paper identifies problems but provides no clear solutions; the 'assisted' experiment merely confirms hand-engineered tools help—an unsurprising result
Missing critical ablations: no Set-of-Marks ablation despite it appearing critical; no systematic analysis of which IDE tools agents actually use; no task difficulty analysis
Contradiction between claims and results: authors claim 'minimal computational overhead' yet evaluation required sampling only 5.5% of the benchmark due to budget constraints

strengths: Comprehensive and well-designed IDE-based environment with proper isolation, checkpointing, and extensibility for evaluating computer-use agents on software engineering tasks
Large-scale diverse benchmark (5,400 instances, 15 tasks, 14+ languages, multiple modalities) unifying existing datasets with novel task categories (IDE Configuration, General-SWE)

Thorough empirical evaluation across multiple agent architectures and models (Gemini, GPT-4, Claude variants, open-weight) with detailed failure mode analysis (visual grounding, tool usage, error recovery)
Detailed quantitative and qualitative analysis of agent limitations with specific metrics (95% of trajectories have grounding errors) and concrete examples of failure patterns
Useful insights about latent model capabilities through prompted tool usage (25%→75% improvement with guidance) and assisted agent experiments (13.3% improvement)
Clear infrastructure contributions with gymnasium API, state checkpointing, and secure dockerized environment enabling reproducibility and future research
Well-positioned relative to prior work with comprehensive comparisons to existing environments and benchmarks
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: environment is primarily VSCode + Docker + xdotool integration with competent engineering but not conceptually novel contributions beyond prior environments like OSWorld

Main empirical finding (pure CUAs significantly underperform specialized agents: 22.9% vs 48.8%) is somewhat expected rather than surprising, with limited evidence supporting the premise that CUAs should be preferred for SWE

Significant evaluation limitations: main results on PwP-Bench-Lite (300 instances, 20 samples per task) with 20-step limit; extended 250-step evaluation relegated to appendix on only 3 datasets with no deep analysis

Extensive documentation of visual grounding failures (95% of trajectories) without proposing solutions or investigating whether fundamental architectural changes could help; Set-of-Marks proven ineffective but not deeply analyzed

Insufficient root cause analysis: documents that CUAs fail but doesn't systematically explore why (e.g., visual grounding vs planning vs task understanding) or whether fine-tuning/prompting/architecture changes could help
Single specialized agent baseline (mini-sweagent) tested; no comparison with recent agents like full SWE-agent, Agentless, or OpenHands-Versa, limiting strength of comparisons
No task difficulty characterization or analysis of why certain tasks achieve 0% performance; task distribution may not reflect real-world SWE proportions

Missing critical ablations: no systematic exploration of grounding improvements, prompt engineering effects, or tool discovery mechanisms; limited investigation of how performance scales with step budget
Fair comparison concerns: best-reported scores acknowledge different experimental setups, inference scaling, and finetuning; only 20 instances per task may not be representative
Limited practical guidance: paper doesn't address when/why practitioners should use CUAs vs specialized agents, or cost-benefit analysis; assisted agent experiment is promising but underexplored
